Virulent

/VEER-yuh-luhnt/ - the stress falls on VEER · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Virulent means extremely severe and destructive in its effects.

The senator's lead evaporated under a virulent whisper campaign that no denial seemed able to slow.

Worked Example

Australia loosed the myxoma virus on its rabbit plague in 1950, and the first summer's numbers stunned even the planners: better than ninety-nine of every hundred infected rabbits died. Nothing in field medicine had seen so lethal an agent. Within a decade, though, the virus itself had mellowed — versions that killed too fast ran out of hosts to carry them — and virologists still teach the story as virulence negotiating with survival.

Virulent is the exact word for that first summer's virus, because it means extremely severe and destructive in its effects — it grades the force of the blow, not the reach. A contagious germ spreads easily; an epidemic one has already spread everywhere; a virulent one hits hard, killing or crippling what it touches. The word travels well, too: criticism and rumors turn virulent when they stop wounding and start destroying.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

deadly: kills — full stop; virulent grades the whole force of the harm, fatal or not

savage: brutally fierce in its attack

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

harmless: doing no damage at all

gentle: soft in its effects

Where it sits · how dangerous the disease is — mild → severe → virulent

mild vs. virulent: A mild strain passes through in a day or two and is soon forgotten.

severe vs. virulent: Severe goes further than mild — beds fill and recoveries drag — but virulent claims the most: a strain so destructive it kills or cripples swiftly.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — vir

Root — vir: poison, venom (Latin virus)

Suffix — -ulent

Suffix — -ulent: full of (as in fraudulent)

Put it together

Put it together: Vir- (poison) + -ulent (full of) = full of poison. Latin virulentus described venomous bites; English aimed it first at diseases that behave like poisons and then at language that does — a virulent attack in print poisons a reputation the way a virulent strain poisons blood.

Use the root in a new word: virus

Use the root in a new word: virus: Latin farm manuals used virus for a serpent's venom and a plant's poisonous sap alike — the word waited two thousand years for germ theory to need it.

Root Check

Word Choice

grave / evaluative

Virulent grades severity — of pathogens literally, of attacks and rumors by extension — and it always means destructive force, not reach. Contagious describes spread; deadly counts only the kills. In this unit it is the adjective among the nouns: a blight or a bane names the destroyer, while virulent tells you how hard it strikes.
